claim: The yeast centrosome (SPB) consists of three major layers: an inner plaque facing the nucleus, a central plaque rooted in the nuclear envelope, and an outer plaque facing the cytoplasm.
source: The SPB consists of three major layers — an inner plaque facing the nucleus, a central plaque rooted in the nuclear envelope and an outer plaque facing the cytoplasm (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, which show the structural organization of the SPB.

claim: The SPB has a specialized extension called the half-bridge that is required for SPB duplication.
source: A specialized extension on one side, the half-bridge, is required for SPB duplication (Byers and Goetsch, 1975).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Byers and Goetsch, 1975.

claim: Microtubule nucleation sites arise by recruitment of the γ-tubulin complex (γTC) composed of Tub4, Spc98/GCP3, and Spc97/GCP2.
source: Microtubule (MT) nucleation sites arise by recruitment of the conserved γ-tubulin complex (γTC but also referred to as the γ-tubulin small complex or γ-TuSC) composed of Tub4 (yeast γ-tubulin), Spc98/GCP3 and Spc97/GCP2 (Farache et al., 2018; Geissler et al., 1996; Knop, 1997a; Kollman et al., 2011; Winey and Bloom, 2012).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with multiple supporting citations.

claim: The inner plaque organizes intranuclear spindle microtubules by docking γTCs onto Spc110/pericentrin.
source: The inner plaque organizes intranuclear spindle MTs by docking γTCs onto Spc110/pericentrin (Knop, 1997b).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text with a supporting citation.

claim: Nucleation of cytoplasmic or astral microtubules occurs from two distinct γTC-docking sites set up by Spc72/CDK5RAP2 upon binding Nud1/centriolin at the outer plaque or Kar1 at the half-bridge.
source: By contrast, nucleation of cytoplasmic or astral microtubules (aMTs) occurs from two distinct γTC-docking sites set up by the cytoplasmic receptor Spc72/CDK5RAP2, upon binding Nud1/centriolin at the outer plaque or Kar1 at the half-bridge (Gruneberg, 2000; Knop and Schiebel, 1998; Lin et al., 2015; Pereira et al., 1999).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text with multiple supporting citations.

claim: SIM can resolve SPB inner and outer plaques using strains expressing endogenous SPB components fused to fluorescent tags.
source: SIM represents an effective approach to answer these questions as demonstrated by a previous study focused on core molecular events in SPB duplication (Burns et al., 2015). Of particular relevance is the ability of SIM to resolve SPB inner and outer plaques shown by that study, using strains expressing endogenous SPB components fused to fluorescent tags.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with a citation to Burns et al., 2015.

claim: Single SPBs of cells expressing Tub4-mTurquoise2 showed two distinct foci that could be assigned to inner and outer plaques by co-label with YFP-Spc110 or YFP-Spc72, respectively.
source: Accordingly, single SPBs of cells expressing Tub4-mTurquoise2 (mT2) showed two distinct foci that could be assigned to inner and outer plaques by co-label with YFP-Spc110 or YFP-Spc72, respectively (Burns et al., 2015 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing the co-localization data.

claim: The focus co-localized with YFP-Spc110 was more intense than the signal co-localized with YFP-Spc72.
source: In all cases, the focus co-localized with YFP-Spc110 was more intense than the signal co-localized with YFP-Spc72, consistent with the idea that there is more γTC at the inner plaque of the SPB than at the outer plaque.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text based on observations from the data.

claim: The overall inner to outer plaque ratio (IP:OP ratio) for γTC components is approximately 2-3.
source: Based on the accepted nuclear to cytoplasmic MT ratio of ~5–10 (Erlemann et al., 2012), we anticipated a similar ratio for the γTC. Against expectations, quantitative analysis uncovered an overall inner to outer plaque ratio (IP:OP ratio) of ~2–3 for each γTC component.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text based on quantitative analysis of SIM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In diploid cells, the number of microtubules increases two-fold compared to haploid cells.
source: In diploid cells, the number of MTs increases two-fold (Byers and Goetsch, 1974).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with a supporting citation.

claim: Analysis of Tub4-mT2 distribution in haploids and diploids showed a roughly two-fold increase in γTC at both the inner and outer plaques of diploid SPBs.
source: Analysis of Tub4-mT2 distribution in haploids and diploids showed a roughly two-fold increase in γTC at both the inner and outer plaques of diploid SPBs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Only approximately 12% of all SPBs in SIM images showed a top view orientation.
source: Judging from the apparent overlap between single Tub4 foci and the core outer plaque component Nud1, only ~12% of all SPBs in our SIM images showed a top view (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The kar1∆15 mutation abrogates Spc72 binding to Kar1, thus precluding γTC localization to the bridge.
source: The kar1∆15 mutation abrogates Spc72 binding to Kar1 (Pereira et al., 1999), thus precluding γTC localization to the bridge.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text with a supporting citation.

claim: Unduplicated SPBs from G1-phase cells exhibited a Tub4 IP:OP ratio between 2 and 3.
source: From these averaged images and their quantitation by linescan analysis (Figure 1B) or from quantitation of individual SPBs (Figure 1C), the structural asymmetry between old versus new SPB was apparent. Unduplicated SPBs from G1-phase cells exhibited a Tub4 IP:OP ratio between 2 and 3 that was also manifest in old SPBs throughout the remaining of the cell cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: The Tub4 IP:OP ratio was highest in new SPBs early in spindle assembly but decreased later in the spindle pathway.
source: By contrast, the ratio was highest in new SPBs early in spindle assembly but decreased later in the spindle pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of averaged images and individual SPBs shown in Figures 1B and 1C.

claim: Tub4-mT2 was apparent at the inner plaque of the new SPB early in spindle assembly (<1 µm-long spindles), before Spc72-Venus or Tub4-mT2 accumulated at the new SPB outer plaque.
source: First, Tub4-mT2 was apparent at the inner plaque of the new SPB early in spindle assembly (<1 µm-long spindles), before Spc72-Venus or Tub4-mT2 accumulated at the new SPB outer plaque (Figure 1D a versus b-e).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Both Spc72 and Tub4 were strongly asymmetric at the cytoplasmic face of the SPB in KAR1 cells or mainly present at the old pole in kar1∆15 cells.
source: Both components were strongly asymmetric at the cytoplasmic face of the SPB in KAR1 cells or mainly present at the old pole in kar1∆15 cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The KAR1 and kar1∆15 samples analyzed showed similar spindle length profiles, confirming that overall spindle dynamics was not affected by the kar1∆15 mutation.
source: The KAR1 and kar1∆15 samples analyzed showed similar spindle length profiles (Figure 1F) confirming that overall spindle dynamics was not affected by the kar1∆15 mutation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Incorporation of Tub4-mT2 onto the new SPB trailed Spc72-Venus, consistent with the idea that Spc72 is needed for γTC recruitment to the outer plaque.
source: Second, incorporation of Tub4-mT2 onto the new SPB trailed Spc72-Venus, consistent with the idea that Spc72 is needed for γTC recruitment to the outer plaque (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Tub4 exhibited a marked asymmetry at the cytoplasmic face of the SPB at early stages of the spindle pathway underpinned by Spc72 distribution.
source: Taken together, Tub4 exhibited a marked asymmetry at the cytoplasmic face of the SPB at early stages of the spindle pathway underpinned by Spc72 distribution.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The bridge-based localization of γTC plays little role in the asymmetry of Tub4 at the cytoplasmic face of the SPB.
source: Further, the bridge-based localization of γTC plays little role in this asymmetry.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the comparison of KAR1 and kar1∆15 cells shown in Figure 1.

claim: Spc72 and Tub4 asymmetry during spindle assembly was observed in the W303 yeast strain background in both individual images and in averaged images grouped by cell cycle/spindle stage.
source: Importantly, Spc72 and Tub4 asymmetry during spindle assembly was also observed in the W303 yeast strain background in both individual images and in averaged images grouped by cell cycle/spindle stage (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Quantitative analysis for relative Tub4 partition between inner and outer plaques by stage and SPB identity confirmed that Tub4 asymmetric recruitment is common to both 15D and W303 strain backgrounds.
source: Quantitative analysis for relative Tub4 partition between inner and outer plaques by stage and SPB identity confirmed that Tub4 asymmetric recruitment is common to both 15D and W303 strain backgrounds (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B–C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B-C.

claim: Validation of Spc72 asymmetry by wide-field fluorescence microscopy analysis in multiple strains indicates that the effects are unlikely related to yeast genetic background and/or SIM.
source: Validation of Spc72 asymmetry by wide-field fluorescence microscopy analysis in multiple strains (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) indicates that the effects are unlikely related to yeast genetic background and/or SIM.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Intrinsic SPB structural and functional asymmetry is a general feature of the budding yeast spindle cycle.
source: Rather, these results demonstrate that intrinsic SPB structural and functional asymmetry is a general feature of the budding yeast spindle cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the validation of Spc72 and Tub4 asymmetry across multiple strain backgrounds.

claim: In early G1, unduplicated SPBs contained two Tub4-Venus foci, the strongest corresponding to the inner plaque.
source: From asynchronous wild type cells coexpressing mT2-Spc110 (to discriminate inner and outer plaque) and Tub4-Venus, we could identify multiple configurations of γTC in G1 cells. In early G1, unduplicated SPBs contained two Tub4-Venus foci, the strongest corresponding to the inner plaque (Figure 2A,a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A,a.

claim: A subset of unduplicated SPBs exhibited an elongated cytoplasmic signal extending beyond the presumed outer plaque, which most likely corresponded to bridge-localized γTC.
source: A subset of unduplicated SPBs exhibited an elongated cytoplasmic signal extending beyond the presumed outer plaque (Figure 2A,b); this most likely corresponded to bridge-localized γTC.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A,b.

claim: In later G1, two foci of Spc110 were apparent along with a second prominent Tub4 focus at the new inner plaque.
source: In later G1, two foci of Spc110 were apparent (Figure 2A,c–d) along with a second prominent Tub4 focus at the new inner plaque, consistent with the idea that Spc110 incorporation occurs after SPB insertion into the nuclear envelope and that Spc110 recruits γTC to the SPB inner plaque.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A,c-d.

claim: Duplicated SPBs remained unseparated in S phase and had a variable cytoplasmic label of Tub4-mT2 extending from the old SPB to the space between the two inner plaques.
source: Duplicated SPBs remained unseparated in S phase (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for a distribution of distances between unseparated SPB pairs) and had a variable cytoplasmic label of Tub4-mT2 extending from the old SPB to the space between the two inner plaques, as shown in the 1-pixel linescans across inner and outer plaques (Figure 2A,c–d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2A,c-d and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: γTC is present on the outer plaque of the old SPB throughout SPB duplication and localizes to varying degrees to the bridge.
source: These data suggest that γTC is present on the outer plaque of the old SPB throughout SPB duplication and localizes to varying degrees to the bridge.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: γTC does not appear to be added to the outer plaque of the new SPB as part of SPB duplication in G1.
source: However, it does not appear to be added to the outer plaque of the new SPB as part of SPB duplication in G1.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: During the satellite stage, Tub4 was observed at the old SPB outer plaque, or favoring the space between the SPB and satellite with a residual signal often apparent at the old SPB outer plaque.
source: During the satellite stage, Tub4 was also observed at the old SPB outer plaque (Figure 2B,a, solid arrowhead), or favoring the space between the SPB and satellite with a residual signal often apparent at the old SPB outer plaque (Figure 2B,b, big and small solid arrowheads, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2B,a-b.

claim: After appearance of the new inner plaque, Tub4 label continued to distribute between the old SPB outer plaque and the bridge.
source: After appearance of the new inner plaque (Figure 2B,c–e), label continued to distribute between those two cytoplasmic locations (solid arrowheads).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2B,c-e.

claim: Label associated with the new SPB outer plaque was not observed during SPB duplication.
source: Label associated with the new SPB outer plaque was not observed.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the analysis of Tub4 distribution shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In kar1∆15 cells, Tub4 retained localization exclusively at the old SPB outer plaque throughout SPB duplication.
source: In kar1∆15 cells Tub4 retained localization exclusively at the old SPB outer plaque throughout (Figure 2B,f–g, solid arrowhead) demonstrating that localization at the center of the SPB pair in KAR1 cells represented nucleation sites at the bridge.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2B,f-g.

claim: Tub4 and by extension γTC localizes to the old SPB and bridge during SPB duplication.
source: Thus, Tub4 and by extension γTC, localizes to the old SPB and bridge during SPB duplication.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the text based on the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The fact that Tub4 is readily detected at the new SPB inner plaque but not at the outer plaque indicates that its asymmetry between cytoplasmic faces of the old versus new SPB is not due to fluorophore maturation.
source: The fact that Tub4 is readily detected at the new SPB inner plaque but not at the outer plaque indicates that its asymmetry between cytoplasmic faces of the old versus new SPB is not due to fluorophore maturation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the observation that Tub4 is present at the new inner plaque but not the outer plaque.

claim: SPB insertion is not the trigger for completion of outer plaque assembly.
source: Further, our data clearly demonstrate that SPB insertion is not the trigger for completion of outer plaque assembly.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data showing that the new SPB outer plaque is not complete at the time of insertion.

claim: Some cells showed single Spc72 label at the old SPB while the majority of cells showed Spc72 label extending from the old SPB to the bridge.
source: Like γTC, we observed two localization patterns. Some cells showed single Spc72 label at the old SPB (Figure 2C,a, arrowhead) while the majority of cells showed Spc72 label extending from the old SPB to the bridge, with label favoring one or the other location (Figure 2C,b–d, big and small arrowheads, respectively) and a small proportion appearing to carry label at the bridge exclusively (Figure 2C,e).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2C,a-e.

claim: The dual site distribution of Spc72 was abrogated in kar1∆15 cells in which label remained at the old SPB.
source: This dual site distribution was abrogated in kar1∆15 cells in which label remained at the old SPB (Figure 2C,f).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2C,f.

claim: An identical result was obtained when Spc72-Venus localization was determined in reference to Nud1-mT2 label.
source: An identical result was obtained when Spc72-Venus localization was determined in reference to Nud1-mT2 label (Figure 2D), which also displays two signals from the satellite stage and throughout duplication (Burns et al., 2015 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The data demonstrated the incomplete assembly of the new SPB outer plaque prior to SPB separation.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrated the incomplete assembly of the new SPB outer plaque prior to SPB separation as depicted in the new model proposed in Figure 2E.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the text and illustrated in the model shown in Figure 2E.

claim: By contrast to the dual distribution detected by linescan analysis for both Tub4 and Spc72 relative to Spc42, Kar1 was exclusively positioned between unseparated Spc42 signals.
source: By contrast to the dual distribution detected by linescan analysis for both Tub4 and Spc72 relative to Spc42 used as reference (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B), Kar1 was exclusively positioned between unseparated Spc42 signals (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C and also see Burns et al., 2015; Seybold et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: Colocalization between Kar1 and the central peak of cytoplasmic Tub4 was abrogated in cells expressing Kar1∆15.
source: Colocalization between Kar1 and the central peak of cytoplasmic Tub4 was abrogated in cells expressing instead Kar1∆15 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Three color imaging experiments confirmed that the central peak of Spc72 or Tub4 co-localized with Kar1 at the bridge in unseparated SPBs.
source: Three color imaging experiments using Venus-Kar1 in addition to Spc42-mCherry and Tub4-mT2 or Spc72-mT2 confirmed that the central peak of Spc72 or Tub4 co-localized with Kar1 at the bridge in unseparated SPBs (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E.

claim: A significant fraction of both Spc72 and Tub4 are maintained at the old SPB, even in the presence of bridge-localized pools of each protein.
source: Importantly, these experiments clearly showed that a significant fraction of both Spc72 and Tub4 are maintained at the old SPB, even in the presence of bridge-localized pools of each protein.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the three-color imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E.

claim: SPB duplication took place in cells with incipient buds.
source: This allowed us to follow synchronous populations proceeding unperturbed along the subsequent cell cycle to ensure we captured and staged all modes of localization during early landmarks of the spindle pathway (Figure 3). SPB duplication took place in cells with incipient buds (Figure 3A,a,b,f), which began SPB separation 15 min later (Figure 3B-D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3A and 3B-D.

claim: SIM analysis of synchronized cells confirmed the inherent asymmetry built into the SPB duplication cycle.
source: SIM analysis of these synchronized cells confirmed the inherent asymmetry built into the SPB duplication cycle, the overall absence of Spc72 and Spc98 at the new SPB outer plaque, and a modest contribution to Spc72 label at the new SPB attributed to the bridge, as inferred from the nearly absolute asymmetry at onset of SPB separation observed in kar1∆15 cells.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the SIM analysis of synchronized cells shown in Figure 3.

claim: Spc72 began to accumulate in short spindles prior to anaphase onset, as indicated by a significant drop in Spc72 asymmetry index at the transition from the ~1 µm long stage.
source: As indicated by a significant drop in Spc72 asymmetry index at the transition from the ~1 µm long stage, Spc72 began to accumulate in short spindles prior to anaphase onset (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Throughout SPB duplication and the ensuing side-by-side stage, Spc72 and the cytoplasmic pool of γTC are present at the old SPB outer plaque and the bridge but are absent from the new SPB outer plaque.
source: In conclusion, throughout SPB duplication and the ensuing side-by-side stage, Spc72 and the cytoplasmic pool of γTC are present at the old SPB outer plaque and the bridge but are absent from the new SPB outer plaque.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: This asymmetry persists at onset of SPB separation with the new SPB acquiring Spc72, and γTC, as cells transit past the ~1 µm-long spindle stage.
source: This asymmetry persists at onset of SPB separation with the new SPB acquiring Spc72, and γTC, as cells transit past the ~1 µm-long spindle stage.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Tethering the γTC-binding domain of Spc72 to Cnm67 abrogates the delay in aMT acquisition by the new SPB during spindle assembly.
source: The observation that tethering the γTC-binding domain of Spc72 to Cnm67 (a component incorporated to the new SPB from the satellite stage) abrogates the delay in aMT acquisition by the new SPB during spindle assembly (Juanes et al., 2013) is consistent with this model.
evidence: This is stated in the text with a supporting citation to Juanes et al., 2013.

claim: Intrinsic SPB asymmetry is abolished in cdc28-4 clb5∆ mutant cells, with both SPBs exhibiting aMTs at onset of SPB separation.
source: Intrinsic SPB asymmetry is also abolished in cdc28-4 clb5∆ mutant cells, with both SPBs exhibiting aMTs at onset of SPB separation (Segal et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the text with a supporting citation to Segal et al., 2000.

claim: Short spindles of wild type and cdc28-4 mutant cells exhibited marked Spc72 asymmetry while a modest decrease was observed in clb5∆ cells.
source: Short spindles of wild type and cdc28-4 mutant cells exhibited marked Spc72 asymmetry while a modest decrease was observed in clb5∆ cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Asymmetry was significantly impaired in cdc28-4 clb5∆ cells.
source: By contrast, asymmetry was significantly impaired in cdc28-4 clb5∆ cells (Figure 4A–B), in agreement with the observation that this mutant nucleates aMTs at both SPBs at onset of spindle assembly (Segal et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: A strong synergy was observed between the cdc28-4 and clb5∆ mutations — in the double mutant, Spc72 was present at the new SPB already before SPB separation in more than 50% of cells analyzed.
source: A strong synergy was observed between the cdc28-4 and clb5∆ mutations — in the double mutant, Spc72 was present at the new SPB already before SPB separation in more than 50% of cells analyzed (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Introducing the kar1∆15 allele did not affect excess symmetry caused by cdc28-4 clb5∆ mutations, confirming the involvement of the new SPB outer plaque.
source: Additionally, introducing the kar1∆15 allele did not affect excess symmetry caused by cdc28-4 clb5∆ mutations confirming the involvement of the new SPB outer plaque (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The genetic interaction was specific for clb5∆ and not shared by a clb3∆ clb4∆ mutant.
source: The genetic interaction was specific for clb5∆ and not shared by a clb3∆ clb4∆ mutant even though Clb3 and Clb4 are needed for timely SPB separation (Juanes et al., 2011; Segal et al., 1998 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The requirement for S-phase CDK in restricting Spc72 to the old SPB during the side-by-side stage was confirmed by SIM analysis of KAR1 or kar1∆15 cells upon induction of a non-degradable version of the CDK inhibitor Sic1.
source: The requirement for S-phase CDK in restricting Spc72 to the old SPB during the side-by-side stage was further confirmed by SIM analysis of KAR1 or kar1∆15 cells upon induction of a non-degradable version of the CDK inhibitor Sic1, which prevents entry into S phase and arrests cells prior to SPB separation (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: S-phase CDK imparts correct spindle polarity by enforcing Spc72 asymmetry.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that S-phase CDK imparts correct spindle polarity by enforcing Spc72 asymmetry.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Only cells expressing Nud17A prompted a significant loss of Spc72 asymmetry in vivo.
source: From those candidates, only cells expressing Nud17A in which positions S21, S294, T388, T392, S469, T806 and T843 were substituted by A to cancel seven CDK consensus sites, prompted a significant loss of Spc72 asymmetry in vivo (Figure 5A–B) despite a slight reduction in Nud1 expression level (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5A-B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mutation of seven CDK consensus sites in Nud1 abolished phosphorylation by purified Clb5-Cdc28-as in vitro.
source: Mutation of these sites abolished phosphorylation by purified Clb5-Cdc28-as in vitro (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Nud17A exhibited reduced bulk phosphorylation relative to wild type Nud1 in vivo.
source: Accordingly, Nud17A exhibited reduced bulk phosphorylation relative to wild type Nud1 in vivo, based on mobility shift assessed by western blot analysis of protein extracts from unperturbed cells or cells depleted of Cdc5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and C, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: Expression of Nud17A increased the percentage of cells in which the new SPB entered the bud.
source: Consistent with this idea, expression of Nud17A increased the percentage of cells in which the new SPB entered the bud (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: nud17A cells exhibited a marked reduction in Spc72 and Spc98 asymmetry at onset of SPB separation.
source: nud17A cells already exhibited a marked reduction in Spc72 and Spc98 asymmetry at onset of SPB separation (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: Spc72 recruitment to the new outer plaque was observed in side-by-side SPBs of nud17A cells.
source: Furthermore, we observed Spc72 recruitment to the new outer plaque in side-by-side SPBs of nud17A cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The phenotype in nud17A cells appeared less penetrant than in cdc28-4 clb5∆ cells, suggesting that while Nud1 may be a key target, other CDK substrates are probably involved.
source: While reminiscent of that observed in cdc28-4 clb5∆ cells, the phenotype appeared less penetrant in nud17A cells (Figure 5G–H), suggesting that while Nud1 may be a key target, other CDK substrates are probably involved.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: CDK treatment resulted in a nearly 10-fold increase in pull-down efficiency for wild type Nud1 but exerted no effect on the extent of Spc72 binding to Nud17A.
source: CDK treatment resulted in a nearly 10-fold increase in pull-down efficiency for wild type Nud1 but exerted no effect on the extent of Spc72 binding to Nud17A (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The interaction between Nud1 and Spc72 and its enhancement by CDK phosphorylation were retained by a Nud1 domain extending between amino acid positions 250–600.
source: The interaction and its enhancement by CDK phosphorylation were retained by a Nud1 domain extending between amino acid positions 250–600 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Both Cln2 and Clb5 as part of CDK complexes were efficiently pulled down by purified Spc72 in vitro.
source: Both Cln2 and Clb5 as part of CDK complexes were efficiently pulled down by purified Spc72 in vitro (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Changes in affinity induced by CDK phosphorylation of Nud1 may enforce Spc72 retention at the old SPB within a temporal window of opportunity initiated by Spc72 itself, thus reinforcing its bias to the old SPB.
source: It follows that changes in affinity induced by CDK phosphorylation of Nud1 may enforce Spc72 retention at the old SPB within a temporal window of opportunity initiated by Spc72 itself, thus reinforcing its bias to the old SPB.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the in vitro binding data and the observation that Spc72 interacts with CDK complexes.

claim: Analysis of Tub4-Venus localization in cdc28-4 clb5∆ cells pointed to comparable intensities of Tub4-Venus at inner versus outer plaque.
source: Surprisingly, this analysis pointed to comparable intensities of Tub4-Venus at inner versus outer plaque in this mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: 5 out of 12 cdc28-4 clb5∆ cells displayed a new Tub4 signal that colocalized with Nud1 at the presumptive new outer plaque before Tub4 presence at the new inner plaque.
source: By contrast, 5 out of 12 cdc28-4 clb5∆ cells displayed a new Tub4 signal that colocalized with Nud1 at the presumptive new outer plaque before Tub4 presence at the new inner plaque (Figure 6A,e versus Figure 6A, f-gA; hollow versus solid white arrowhead).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6A,e-g.

claim: cdc28-4 clb5∆ cells might complete the assembly of the new SPB outer plaque before the new inner plaque is fully established, a reversal of the wild type sequence of events.
source: These data suggested that cdc28-4 clb5∆ cells might complete the assembly of the new SPB outer plaque before the new inner plaque is fully established, a reversal of the wild type sequence of events.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: cdc28-4 clb5∆ mutant cells exhibited both significant accumulation of Tub4 at the new SPB outer plaque and an overall reduction in Tub4 IP:OP ratio at both SPBs.
source: Yet, cdc28-4 clb5∆ (KAR1 or kar1∆15) mutant cells exhibited both significant accumulation of Tub4 at the new SPB outer plaque and an overall reduction in Tub4 IP:OP ratio at both SPBs.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on analysis of averaged images shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The advanced Tub4 incorporation at the outer plaque relative to the inner plaque at the side-by-side stage was further apparent by analyzing individual images.
source: By analyzing individual images used for these averages, the advanced Tub4 incorporation at the outer plaque relative to the inner plaque at the side-by-side stage was further apparent (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Advanced Tub4 addition at the outer plaque before inner plaque complete assembly followed Spc72 recruitment.
source: This advanced Tub4 addition at the outer plaque before inner plaque complete assembly followed Spc72 recruitment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Tub4-Venus inner to outer plaque ratio in nud17A cells was essentially unaffected.
source: Contrary to what was observed in cdc28-4 clb5∆ cells, Tub4-Venus inner to outer plaque ratio in nud17A cells was essentially unaffected (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The nud17A mutation was insufficient to reverse the normal sequence for addition of Tub4 recruitment during assembly of the new SPB.
source: Although the nud17A mutation perturbed Tub4 asymmetry at the side-by-side stage in line with the advanced recruitment of Spc72 at the new SPB outer plaque (Figure 5), it was insufficient to reverse the normal sequence for addition of Tub4 recruitment during assembly of the new SPB (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Inactivation of S-phase CDK in cdc28-4 clb5∆ cells not only abrogated asymmetry otherwise arising from the SPB duplication cycle but also reversed the orderly sequence of events required to build the new SPB, with concomitant impact on the balanced recruitment of the γTC to each SPB face.
source: Taken together, inactivation of S-phase CDK in cdc28-4 clb5∆ cells not only abrogated asymmetry otherwise arising from the SPB duplication cycle but also reversed the orderly sequence of events required to build the new SPB, with concomitant impact on the balanced recruitment of the γTC to each SPB face.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 6.

claim: CDK helps retain Spc72 at the old SPB outer plaque thus enforcing asymmetry in unseparated SPBs, at least in part, via phosphorylation of Nud1.
source: First, CDK helps retain Spc72 at the old SPB outer plaque thus enforcing asymmetry in unseparated SPBs, at least in part, via phosphorylation of Nud1.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data presented in Figures 4-6.

claim: CDK imposes the sequential addition and the ensuing distribution of γTC at the inner and outer plaques, most likely, by phosphorylation of other SPB components.
source: Second, CDK further imposes the sequential addition and the ensuing distribution of γTC at the inner and outer plaques, most likely, by phosphorylation of other SPB components (see Discussion).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 6.

claim: These findings point to critical links between CDK temporal control, correct SPB morphogenesis and functional asymmetry.
source: These findings point to critical links between CDK temporal control, correct SPB morphogenesis and functional asymmetry.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the data presented in the Results section.

claim: The current work challenges the idea that completion of the new outer plaque, specifically addition of Spc72 and γTC, temporally precedes SPB insertion and even separation in wild type cells.
source: Yet, our current work challenges the idea that completion of the new outer plaque, specifically addition of Spc72 and γTC, temporally precedes SPB insertion and even separation in wild type cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion based on the data presented.

claim: Spc72 and γTC are added later as the new SPB matures part-way along spindle assembly.
source: Rather, these distal components are added later as the new SPB matures part-way along spindle assembly.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion based on the data presented.

claim: The availability of γTC is not the sole regulator of MT formation in the cell.
source: This apparent discrepancy between γTC levels and MT nucleation suggests that the availability of γTC is not the sole regulator of MT formation in the cell.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion based on the observed IP:OP ratio.

claim: CDK may act through further substrates at the SPB, and more broadly via other protein kinases such as Mps1 and Cdc5, both dependent on CDK for their activity.
source: Thus, CDK may act through further substrates at the SPB, and more broadly via other protein kinases such as Mps1 and Cdc5, both dependent on CDK for their activity (Jaspersen et al., 2004; Mortensen et al., 2005; Rodriguez-Rodriguez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Clb5-Cdc28 might antagonize Cdc14 by direct phosphorylation.
source: Finally, Clb5-Cdc28 might antagonize Cdc14 by direct phosphorylation (Li et al., 2014), while the interplay between CDK thresholds and a constellation of phosphatases acting at the G1/S boundary is beginning to emerge (Ariño et al., 2019; Martín et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: CDK phosphorylation prompts maturation of the new inner plaque ahead of the outer plaque.
source: Thus, CDK phosphorylation prompts maturation of the new inner plaque ahead of the outer plaque.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion based on the data and known CDK targets.

claim: In cdc28-4 clb5∆ cells, the combined effect of advanced Spc72 association with the new outer plaque and impaired retention of γTC by the inner plaque through hypophosphorylation of Spc110, Spc98 and Tub4 might cause roughly concurrent binding of γTC to both faces of the SPB with concomitant decrease in the IP:OP ratio.
source: In cdc28-4 clb5∆ cells, the combined effect of advanced Spc72 association with the new outer plaque and impaired retention of γTC by the inner plaque through hypophosphorylation of Spc110, Spc98 and Tub4 might cause roughly concurrent binding of γTC to both faces of the SPB with concomitant decrease in the IP:OP ratio.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a mechanistic explanation for the observed phenotype.

claim: CDK-enforced orderly SPB assembly ensures both correct SPB morphogenesis and age-dependent structural asymmetry.
source: In conclusion, CDK-enforced orderly SPB assembly ensures both correct SPB morphogenesis and age-dependent structural asymmetry.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion based on all the data presented.

claim: Temporally asymmetric aMT organization is a hallmark of spindle polarity in yeast with the pole initially carrying aMTs, the old SPB, becoming the bud-ward pole.
source: Temporally asymmetric aMT organization is a hallmark of spindle polarity in yeast —with the pole initially carrying aMTs, the old SPB, becoming the bud-ward pole (Pereira et al., 2001; Segal et al., 2000; Shaw et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Extrinsic asymmetries function in two key processes promoting spindle polarity: aMT capture by the polarity determinant Bud6 at the bud cell cortex and Kar9-dependent delivery of aMT plus ends to the bud along actin cables.
source: Extrinsic asymmetries function in two key processes promoting spindle polarity: aMT capture by the polarity determinant Bud6 at the bud cell cortex and Kar9-dependent delivery of aMT plus ends to the bud along actin cables (Geymonat and Segal, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Both extrinsic determinants are necessary but insufficient to link SPB age, identity and fate without intrinsic SPB asymmetry.
source: However, both extrinsic determinants are necessary but insufficient to link SPB age, identity and fate without intrinsic SPB asymmetry (Cepeda-García et al., 2010; Huisman et al., 2004; Juanes et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Intrinsic SPB asymmetry cannot translate into asymmetric fate unless aMTs from the old SPB are targeted to the bud cell cortex through extrinsic cues.
source: Conversely, intrinsic SPB asymmetry cannot translate into asymmetric fate unless aMTs from the old SPB are targeted to the bud cell cortex through extrinsic cues.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as a conclusion based on the interplay between intrinsic and extrinsic factors.

claim: In bud6∆ or kar9∆ mutants, aMT temporal asymmetry during spindle assembly is still manifest (and therefore intrinsic) but no longer determines the pole ending in the bud.
source: Indeed, in bud6∆ or kar9∆ mutants, aMT temporal asymmetry during spindle assembly is still manifest (and therefore intrinsic) but no longer determines the pole ending in the bud (Yeh et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: aMTs are differentially stabilized by cell compartment through cortical cues: interaction between Bim1 at aMT plus ends and cortical Bud6 stabilizes cortical contacts and aMTs are stabilized during Kar9-mediated transport toward the bud.
source: Furthermore, aMTs are differentially stabilized by cell compartment through those same cortical cues: interaction between Bim1 (yeast EB1) at aMT plus ends and cortical Bud6 stabilizes cortical contacts (Ten Hoopen et al., 2012) and aMTs are stabilized during Kar9-mediated transport toward the bud (Huisman et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The interplay between spatial control of distribution of the nucleation machinery and cell cycle-dependent phosphorylation may turn out a recurrent theme in centrosome control and beyond given the conservation of these nucleation systems and the protein kinase regulatory networks promoting maturation.
source: The interplay between spatial control of distribution of the nucleation machinery and cell cycle-dependent phosphorylation may turn out a recurrent theme in centrosome control and beyond given the conservation of these nucleation systems and the protein kinase regulatory networks promoting maturation (Fu et al., 2015; Tovey and Conduit, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion with supporting citations.
